newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Spanish banks to secure new sprawling LATAM empire.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Spanish banks to secure new sprawling LATAM empire.

text.p: Having helped themselves to huge chunks of Latin American banking recently, Spanish banks must now get to work and whip their far-flung holdings into shape.
Since mid-December, market leaders Santander and Banco Bilbao Vizcaya have ploughed some $2.1 billion into Latin America in a whirlwind buying binge through Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Venezuela.

This latest shopping spree, following an acquisitive 1996, brought their combined investment in the region to some $5.3 billion with assets of $62.9 billion following more than a dozen purchases a piece this decade.
"They have made a very heavy investment effort and now they have to consolidate what they have," said Jose Sevilla, banking analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
"They've bought a ton of institutions with lots of personnel and now they have to manage them."
Although a few, possibly major, purchases may still lie ahead, analysts believe the two banks will pause now to digest their holdings and ensure they can provide the promised returns.
"There could be one or two (more purchases) but now they are consolidating operations," another Madrid-based analyst said.

Question marks remain as to whether BBV will make a purchase in Brazil, the leading Latin American market with the top three banks of the region, after Santander's purchase this year of 51 percent of Banco Geral de Comercio.
Another open matter, analysts say, is whether Spain's third-largest bank, Argentaria will join the fray.
Argentaria, still 29.2 percent state-owned and due for further privatisation, has some 299 billion pesetas ($2 billion) available for purchases.
"In Latin America, we have been studying, and are continuing to study, possible acquistions," a bank spokesman told Reuters.
And analysts also wonder whether Spain's fourth-largest bank, Banco Central Hispano, might increase its Argentine presence.
BCH has invested some $487 million to become the biggest banker in Chile and take a stake in Mexico's Grupo Bital.
SOUTH AMERICAN NETWORK
Through Banco O'Higgins Central Hispano (OHCH), it also owns a network of banks in southern South America including a small bank in Argentina, Banco Tornquist, formerly of Credit Lyonnais.
BCH, with its last purchase in 1996, has already settled in to consolidating its operations and now Spain's two big rivals must do the same if they are deliver expected benefits.

In an interview with Reuters earlier this month, BBV subdirector Ignacio Sanchez-Asiain Sanz said the bank expects a return on equity of at least 20 percent, well above the 14 percent threshhold it sets in the less risky Spanish market.
In the near future, it wants foreign business to represent 25 percent of profits.

"Our strategy is to be a universal bank and we believe that this only makes sense and will only be profitable if one has a position of leadership...When the market matures, if we are not among the banks of reference we will never be profitable," Sanchez-Asiain said.
For its part, Santander has said it eventually hopes to have 50 percent of its earnings through Latin America.
But the Latin American stampede is certainly not without risk. Like others, some Spanish banks ventured into the region two decades ago only to retrench as the debt crisis struck.
"All expansion has to be measured through time," said Argentaria chairman Francisco Gonzalez in March, referring to his rivals headlong plunge into the New World.
At present, a worst-case scenario looks remote. Neither the economy, nor the banks, appear overly risk-laden. And the region has made a solid recovery from the 1994 Mexican peso crisis.
But as a result of the heavy diet of purchases, U.S. ratings agency Standard & Poor's changed its rating outlook for Santander to negative from stable in late May.
Last October, it left BBV at stable, but added that 1995 and 1996 Latin American purchases had increased the group's overall risk profile.
Nevertheless the shares of the two big banks have certainly not been troubled by the aggressive buys, with the markets eye firmly fixed on earnings potential.
Both outpaced soaring stock index gains of nearly 45 percent since mid-December, with BBV shares up 79 percent in the same time period and Santander's rising a whopping 94 percent.
LATIN AMERICA AN ALTERNATIVE TO EUROPE
Besides, top bankers point out, failing to invest in Latin America may be a greater risk than being there.
At home, Spanish banks face dramatically falling margins, as well as dwindling revenues and increased competition from the scheduled launch of the European single currency in 1999.
With the European market saturated, Spanish banks are turning to Latin America, where cultural affinities give them an edge.
"Diversification is a response to Europe," said a top official at a leading Spanish bank said.

Bank margins, the income banks glean on the difference between the interest rate they pay depositors and the one they charge lenders, have fallen to just under two percent and bankers believe they may narrow to 1.5 percent in the next three years.
In Latin America, average margins are almost triple that and are unlikely to narrow in the near future.
"We could have some 15 years before the margins fall to really tough levels," Sanchez-Asiain said.
Ultimately, success depends on the banks handling their holdings prudently to squeeze the most out of these margins.
"(Success) depends on their management," an analyst said. ($ = 145.9 Spanish Pesetas)
